protections: P1 anti-forgery: an inbound admin-console request that causes a privileged admin REST operation must carry a per-request proof of intent (anti-forgery token or origin/referrer check); the FORM-auth session cookie alone must not authorize it (web.xml:180-188, 219-226; AdminConsoleAuthModule.java:169-182; no inbound token or CSRF filter anywhere: web.xml:94-105 is the only filter and it is mapped to FacesServlet only).

P2 endpoint integrity: the admin REST bearer token held in the console session (AdminConsoleAuthModule.java:214-217) must only be sent to the console's own server-derived REST endpoint, never to a base address supplied by the request (RestUtil.java:831-835, 841-846, 992-997 vs LogFilesContentSource.java:89-94, LogViewerContentSource.java:84-91, ClientStubsContentSource.java:87-92, AdminCallbackHandler.java:189-203).

P3 representation control: the response Content-Type/extension must be chosen by the server-side ContentSource, not by a request parameter (DownloadServlet.java:400-414 falls back to request.getParameter for any Context attribute, and DownloadServlet.java:254-266 consumes ContentType/extension when writing the response header).

P4 path shape: values concatenated into the outbound admin REST path or into server-side file names must be constrained to the shape the console generates (ClientStubsContentSource.java:92, 97-100; LogFilesContentSource.java:99-104; LogViewerContentSource.java:91-94).

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The route is called /download/* and only streams a file back to the browser, and the container already enforces an admin-role FORM-auth constraint on /* (web.xml:180-188) with a re-applied saved Subject on every request (AdminConsoleAuthModule.java:178-182), so the session cookie looks like the intended gate.
The console only ever issues GET for downloads, so POST looks like an internal detail of doGet and a GET-only method rule looks sufficient; the mapping has no http-method restriction either way.

They are three pluggable ContentSource implementations registered by an init-param; each one just opens a stream to download, and the servlet looks like the single place to guard, so the per-source request handling reads as ordinary download plumbing.
These are shared Jersey client helpers written for JSF handlers; authorization is the caller's job, and the servlet is the caller that should be checking, so the shared layer looks exempt.

restUrl is a routing hint that the console's own pages always set to sessionScope.REST_URL (domainLogs.jsf:141, logViewerRaw.jsf:67, subComponentTable.inc:89), so it reads as a trusted internal value; removing it looks like it would break proxy and deployment layouts.

ContentType and extension only pick a MIME type for a file that is about to be saved; they are documented as Context attributes set by the ContentSource, so the request-parameter fallback in Context.getAttribute reads as a convenience and the header write looks cosmetic.

appName, target and instanceName are chosen from console drop-downs and pagination links, so they read as enumerations of known resources rather than free text, and the request only reaches this code once an admin is logged in.

masking: Fixing T5 by making restUrl optional and defaulting to the session REST_URL leaves T1 fully reachable (a cross-site request simply omits restUrl), so the CSRF route becomes invisible rather than closed.
Fixing T1 with a per-request token stops the cross-site path into T5, but the request-controlled outbound endpoint is still there; a test that only exercises the token will not catch it.
T7 stays reachable after both a T1 and a T5 fix because appName/target/instanceName are still concatenated into the REST path and the server-side file names.
T4 is an alternative fix site for the whole T1-T3 group: a check added in RestUtil's *FromServlet helpers would cover every current caller, but no such check exists at either layer.

conflicts.what: The natural T1 fix (require POST, a request-body token, a custom header, or SameSite=Strict) breaks the cross-page GET downloads that are the legitimate use of the very pages that supply T5's restUrl value (domainLogs.jsf:141-154, logViewerRaw.jsf:67, subComponentTable.inc:89).

A T5 fix that rejects or rewrites the download query string wholesale also drops the target/appName/instanceName parameters that T7's legitimate callers depend on; the two need separate decisions (endpoint source vs path-segment validation).

fairness_risks: Legitimate console downloads are opened as cross-page GET navigations (iframe.src and window.location) carrying query parameters: appserver/admingui/common/src/main/resources/appServer/domainLogs.jsf:141-154, likely the most important one; logViewer/logViewerRaw.jsf:67; applications/subComponentTable.inc:89. Any security rule that requires POST, a body-carried token, a custom request header or SameSite=Strict contradicts behaviour these downloads need.

All three pages pass restUrl=#{sessionScope.REST_URL} (encoded on logViewerRaw.jsf), so a rule that rejects a request-supplied restUrl before the pages are updated breaks every log-file, log-view and client-stub download.
The ContentSources init-param (web.xml:119-126) is a servlet extension point; refusing request-parameter ContentType/extension could break content sources shipped outside this repository.

appName and instanceName are user-selected but legal Payara deployment/instance names (domainLogs.jsf:141, subComponentTable.inc:89); an over-broad rejection of separators or slashes can refuse names a real domain accepts.

design.why: Four independent judgements in one servlet surface, each with a different reason to leave it alone: T1 is the CSRF hole on /download/* (absent protection hidden behind an admin-only FORM-auth constraint and a read-only-sounding route, deepseek-type); T5 is the request-chosen REST base that the session's bearer token is attached to, coupled to three JSF pages that must keep passing the same value (mimo-type, and the one site a token-only fix misses); T6 is the Context attribute falling back to request parameters so ContentType/extension steer the response header; T7 is unvalidated appName/target/instanceName concatenated into the REST path and into server-side file names. A single guard closes T1/T2/T3/T4 (hence one group), but it does not touch T5, T6 or T7, and a T5 fix does not touch T1 unless the token is actually implemented. T5 and T6/T7 are the least report-visible and give the stack its depth; T1 provides the in-family anchor. Caveat: T6 and T7 are in-file/in-route siblings rather than members of the CSRF family, so a grader that requires every stacked trap to be the advisory's own CWE should read this candidate as 2 groups (T1, T5) and not as a 4-trap stack.
